name: Dihydroxyacetone

lead: Dihydroxyacetone (DHA) is a simple three-carbon sugar and the active ingredient in virtually all sunless tanning lotions, sprays and mousses. It is produced commercially by fermentation or chemical conversion of glycerol.

In looksmaxxing it is the standard way to add a tan without UV exposure. It gives a temporary golden-brown colour that fades over several days as the outer skin sheds. It provides little or no sun protection, so it does not replace sunscreen.

paras: DHA reacts with free amino groups of proteins and amino acids in the stratum corneum through the Maillard reaction, forming brown pigments called melanoidins. The colour is therefore a surface stain rather than a change in melanin production, and it fades as the keratinised cells exfoliate.

Topical use is considered low risk and DHA is a permitted colour additive for external application in the US. Reviews note it should not be ingested or inhaled, so spray-booth use needs eye, mouth and nose protection, and that long-term and inhalation safety data are limited. Skin irritation or contact allergy is uncommon. A bigger practical risk is false confidence about sun protection, since the tan does not shield against UV.
